title: Abba Moses and the leaking basket
hook: asked to judge a brother, he arrives carrying a basket leaking sand: my own faults run out behind me (Sayings of the Desert Fathers)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elephant in the dark, from Rumi's Masnavi: a pipe, a fan, a pillar, a throne, and Rumi's candle. Your line was bring a candle. Did you ask someone how they see it? Day seventy-three.

Someone messes up, and the group chat lights up. Did you hear what he did? Can you believe she said that? Everybody has an opinion, and it's a strange kind of fun, deciding together how wrong someone else was. Now move the same scene to the Egyptian desert, among the early Christian monks. A community of monks has gathered to sit in judgment on one of their brothers. They're only waiting for one more elder to arrive, a big, famous old man named Moses. And when he finally walks in, he's carrying something odd. Today's story is Abba Moses and the leaking basket.
screen: `DID YOU HEAR WHAT HE DID?` → `THE MONKS GATHER TO JUDGE.` → `ONE ELDER IS LATE.`

segments.voice: Early Christian monks went out into the deserts of Egypt to live simply and pray. They called their elders abba, father, and the elders' short, sharp sayings were remembered and later written down. Those collections are called the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, and they're still read in monasteries today. Abba Moses is a surprising figure in them. Tradition says he came from Ethiopia, was once a servant, and then the leader of a gang of robbers, before he turned up at a monastery and slowly became one of its gentlest elders. Here's the story. A brother at the settlement of Scetis does something wrong. The monks call a council and send for Moses. He doesn't want to come. They send again: everyone is waiting for you. So he gets up and goes. And as he walks in, he's carrying a container full of holes, and something is running out of it behind him the whole way. In the Greek sayings, it's a jug, leaking water. Later retellings make it a basket, trickling sand. The monks come out to meet him and ask: father, what is this? And Moses says, more or less: my own faults are running out behind me, and I don't even see them, and today I've come to judge somebody else's. That's all. And the story says the monks said nothing more to the brother, and forgave him. Notice he doesn't say the brother did nothing wrong. He doesn't give a speech about mercy. He just walks in carrying the truth about himself, where everyone can see it. And the room changes. The trail behind him is the whole sermon.
screen: `THE DESERT FATHERS OF EGYPT.` · `MOSES, ONCE A ROBBER.` · `A CONTAINER FULL OF HOLES.` · `MY FAULTS RUN OUT BEHIND ME.` · then, large: `MY OWN BASKET LEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: skip one judgment today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've been quietly judging. Maybe a coworker, maybe a relative, maybe a stranger online. Don't argue with the judgment; just notice it. Now picture yourself walking toward them carrying Moses's basket, with a thin line of sand running out behind you: a few of your own old mistakes, the ones you'd rather nobody mentioned. Keep walking, and feel what happens to the judgment. You don't have to drop it. Just carry the basket alongside it. The bell holds the time.
Scetis. The desert settlement where an elder came to a trial carrying his own faults behind him, in a basket that leaked the whole way.
Your line: my own basket leaks. Today, the next time you're about to judge someone out loud, remember the sand running out behind you, and say nothing instead. Day seventy-three.

howItsDone: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers are read in Orthodox, Coptic, Catholic and some Protestant communities, and Abba Moses is honored as a saint; the leaking basket is often told when people talk about not judging.

original.note: Aramaic: father. the desert monks used abba as the title for a respected elder.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old monk who didn't notice his basket was broken.
what it means: he carries his own faults in plain sight, so he won't judge another's.
what a scholar hears: in the Greek sayings it's a leaking jug of water, and the council forgives the brother.
